idiom_name: Coordinator objects owning navigation (UINavigationController + child coordinators)
implementation_notes: The community's answer in Swift is the Coordinator pattern: navigation ownership moves out of the view controllers into plain classes - a coordinator holds the navigation controller (or window) and its child coordinators, exposes start(), and decides which screen comes next, so pushViewController/present calls happen in exactly one place per flow. That is the classic Application Controller with delegation instead of a framework: the flow's steps are the coordinator's methods, the commands are the model calls those methods make, and the views stay reusable because they never decide where to go. Keep one coordinator per flow (child coordinators only for genuinely nested subflows) and let views report events through delegates or closures; for SwiftUI prefer the state-driven variant below, and for large guarded graphs consider a formal machine (GameplayKit GKStateMachine or a reducer-based architecture) rather than more branching inside a coordinator.
pitfalls: A coordinator holding its children while the children hold it back leaks the whole flow; keep childCoordinators and clear them in finish(), and let views talk back through weak delegates or closures.
A coordinator per screen just moves navigation around; one coordinator per flow, with children only where a genuine subflow exists.
Nothing enforces the coordinator - a view controller can still push a screen through a storyboard segue, so segues and direct navigations must be removed or the flow has two owners.

variants.name: SwiftUI NavigationStack bound to a NavigationPath
variants.idiom_name: NavigationStack(path:) + navigationDestination(for:) over a Route enum
variants.implementation_notes: In SwiftUI the flow state is the navigation state: NavigationStack binds to a NavigationPath (or to a typed array of routes), steps append or remove values, and navigationDestination(for:) resolves each value to a view, so the central decision becomes the function that mutates the path and deep links are just path construction in onOpenURL. This replaces the coordinator objects - there is no navigator to own - and makes the flow declarative and inspectable; what it gives up is enforcement, since the path accepts whatever value is appended, so a Route enum plus one resolve function is what keeps the conversation legal.
pitfalls: NavigationPath is type-erased: appending an unexpected value is not a compile error, so prefer a typed array of a Route enum and let the resolve function decide what each case shows.
State restoration is manual: a persisted path must be decoded back into routes and validated against the current build, otherwise a restored session can point at screens that no longer exist.
